item.title: In prison, wheelchair basketball offers a chance at reinvention
item.description:
Before basketball practice begins, Larry Roach calls the men into a circle. It’s a Wednesday afternoon, and they are gathering inside the gym at the California Medical Facility, a prison about 55 miles from San Francisco for men, including those with physical disabilities and other serious health needs. The men come in a mix, some rolling in in the wheelchairs they use every day, others walking in. They ease, one by one, into the low chairs with slanted wheels built for basketball. Roach waits until everyone, at least 15 players and five coaches, settles. He is incarcerated here, too, and able-bodied, but in this gym, he has another role: the “inside” coach. item.title: Alaska Senate Candidates Rarely Mention Climate Change, But They Talk a Lot About Fish
item.description:
This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. If you listen to the candidates running for the US Senate seat in Alaska, some of the biggest issues in the race revolve around the state’s fisheries, its oil and gas development, and soaring prices for fuel and other staples. Left largely unsaid, however, is that climate change is playing a role in at least two of these issues. Warming waters are affecting the state’s fish, including declining salmon runs. Concerns for climate change are a chief cause of opposition to expanded oil and gas development in the Alaskan Arctic, where rapid warming is melting permafrost, damaging infrastructure and altering animal migrations that many Alaska Natives rely on for subsistence. Yet the candidates have hardly mentioned climate change. And that might be one of the few ways…

item.description:

It's a not-so-clever way of trimming back the Constitution's protections. item.title: AI Colonies Are Coming
item.description:
—inkoly—Getty Images Each new release of a frontier AI model , such as Anthropic’s Mythos or OpenAI’s Astra , brings a new wave of speculation over how much closer this takes us to artificial general intelligence (AGI) and how much further that lofty goal remains. But what if we’re overlooking something more important than an individual model’s supposed IQ? OpenAI recently announced that an internal model, claimed to be “significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra,” solved Navier-Stokes, one of a handful of legendary math problems each carrying a million-dollar bounty. While mathematicians unpack what this means for the profession, and investors unpack what it means for OpenAI’s upcoming IPO, to me the biggest takeaway is that capability emerges from the collective. item.title: America Is Spending Billions To Fight the War on Terror in Africa. The Terrorists Are Winning.
item.description:
The first state to be ruled by Al Qaeda might not be in Afghanistan or the Arab world—and its ruler might be a former whiskey-drinking rock star. In April, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims ("JNIM" in Arabic) led an uprising in the African nation of Mali, killing Defense Minister Sadio Camara, breaking open a prison holding thousands of inmates, and besieging Bamako, the capital. The fighting was still underway as of August. Mali is not the only place threatened by a JNIM takeover. The West African branch of Al Qaeda is active in a belt of countries known as the Sahel. Its leader, Iyad Ag Ghali, was the former percussionist for the rock band Tinariwen . He now leads a campaign to stamp out the " music of Satan ." item.title: Trump administration has pushed off 13% of Americans enrolled in food stamps
item.description:
A heated debate over how to define what qualifies as an ultra-processed food contributed to the resignation of Trump administration health adviser Calley Means ahead of the midterm elections. People familiar with his exit say he was frustrated with a lack of progress toward the release of a white paper with a proposed definition. Means blamed ultra-processed foods for the “ chronic disease crisis ” in the US. But the food industry has raised concerns over what impact the forthcoming proposed definition could have on lawsuits across the country, and the White House is still scheduled to meet separately with several groups to discuss the issue in the coming weeks — including the National Restaurant Association on Tuesday , the Center for Food Safety on Thursday , and the Consumer Brands Association and Flavor and Extract Manufacturers Association in the days after the midterms. — David Lim
